## Today's question

On day 6 you typed plant lengths by hand. The real experiment has 24 seedlings,
and their lengths are in `data/seedlings.csv`. Can we bring that table into R
unchanged, and check that it holds what we think it holds: 24 plants, two
groups, two lengths each?

The study is described in the data dictionary,
[`data/README.md`](../data/README.md): 24 seedlings in separate pots, 12
randomly allocated to a nutrient treatment and 12 to a control, each measured at
the start and after seven days, in millimetres. These are simulated teaching
data. Keep the dictionary open; R can count rows, but only the dictionary tells
you what a row means.

Open `introcomputing.Rproj` and create a new script, `day07.R`, in the project
folder.

**Save today:** `day07.R`.

## Is R looking in the right folder?

Use `getwd()` and `file.exists()` to find out whether R can see the seedling file:

```{r}
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
```

`getwd()` prints the folder R is working in, which should be your project folder,
not `data`. The second line should print `TRUE`. The path `data/seedlings.csv`
starts from the project folder, so the same line works on a classmate's computer,
even though their full path is different.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: `file.exists()` says `FALSE`

You have probably opened a different project, a project inside a ZIP preview, or
a folder with an extra level from extraction. Open `introcomputing.Rproj` from the
folder where `data`, `output` and `reports` sit side by side. Do not paste your
own full path into the code; it would break on every other computer.
:::

## Reading the CSV into R

The `readr` package provides `read_csv()`, which reads a CSV file into a table.
A **package** is a collection of extra functions. It is installed once (see the
[software setup page](../intro/r-rstudio.qmd)) and loaded with `library()` in
every new R session.

```{r}
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)
```

The table is now an object called `seedlings` in R's memory; the file on disk is
unchanged. `head()` shows its first six rows. `dim()` gives **24 rows and 4
columns**, so all 24 plants arrived. `names()` lists the columns, `plant_id`,
`treatment`, `initial_mm` and `final_mm`, and `str()` shows their types:
`plant_id` and `treatment` are text (`chr`), the two lengths are numbers (`num`).
`show_col_types = FALSE` only hides a message; it does not check anything for you.

Read the first row aloud: plant **P01**, in the **control** group, was **25.7 mm**
at the start and **44.3 mm** seven days later. Each row is one plant and each
column one variable. The two lengths in a row are the same plant measured twice,
so the table describes 24 plants, not 48.

## One column at a time

`$` takes one column out of the table as a vector, like those you made on day 6:

```{r}
seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)
```

There are 24 initial lengths, one per plant, and their mean is **22.47 mm**. The
unit comes from the dictionary: the file only contains numbers. This mean mixes
both groups, so it says nothing yet about the treatment.

## Missing values

When a measurement was never made, R shows `NA`, "not available". It is not
a zero: a seedling of length 0 mm is a different thing from a seedling nobody
measured.

```{r}
mean(c(10, NA, 20))
mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE)
mean(c(10, 0, 20))
```

The first mean is `NA`, because R will not pretend it knows the missing value.
`na.rm = TRUE` asks R to leave it out, which gives **15** from the two values that
exist. Writing 0 instead gives **10**, from three values, one of which was
invented. When you leave missing values out, say how many there were.

## The seedling table

Add each step to `day07.R` with a short comment giving the answer.

1. Use `tail(seedlings)` to find out which group the last plant, P24, belongs to.
   It is **treated**, with lengths 22.4 and 44.7 mm.
2. Use `sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))` to find out how many plants have no final
   length. The answer is **0**: `is.na()` gives `TRUE` for each missing value and
   `sum()` counts them.
3. The file `data/leaf-mass.csv` comes from a different study. Read it into an
   object called `leaves`, and use `dim()`, `names()` and the dictionary to find
   out what one row is. It has **18 rows and 3 columns**: one leaf from each of 18
   plants, with its area in cm² (`leaf_area_cm2`) and dry mass in mg
   (`dry_mass_mg`).
4. Restart R (**Session → Restart R**) and run `day07.R` from the top. Everything
   should come back, and the CSV files are still exactly as supplied.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: `could not find function "read_csv"`

Run `library(readr)` first; after a restart it has to be run again. If R says
there is no package called `readr`, install it as on the setup page. For column
names, copy them from `names(seedlings)`: `initial_mm` works, `initial` does not.
:::

## A second class's data

Another class repeated the experiment with 18 seedlings, in
`data/seedlings-transfer.csv`. According to the dictionary, it has the same
columns, 9 plants per group, and lengths in mm measured seven days apart. Before
you use someone else's table, check that it matches that description. Create
`day07-inspection.R` for this part.

1. Read the file into a new object, `transfer`, so that your `seedlings` table is
   not overwritten. Use `dim()` to find out how many plants it has: **18 rows, 4
   columns**.
2. Use `length(unique(transfer$plant_id))` to find out whether any plant appears
   twice. `unique()` keeps each ID once, so 18 distinct IDs in 18 rows means
   every row is a different plant.
3. Use `table(transfer$treatment)` to find out how many plants are in each group:
   **9 control and 9 treated**, as promised.
4. Use `sum(is.na())` on both length columns to find out whether any length is
   missing (none is), and `range()` to find out whether the lengths look like
   seedlings in mm: initial **20.0 to 28.8 mm**, final **36.0 to 46.2 mm**.
5. Write what you found in `reports/transfer-import-audit.txt`, as sentences
   someone else can check. For example: "`data/seedlings-transfer.csv`: 18 rows ×
   4 columns, 18 distinct plant IDs, 9 control and 9 treated, no missing lengths.
   Lengths in mm, seven days apart (from the dictionary)."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: `transfer$initial` gives `NULL`

The column is called `initial_mm`. Copy names from `names(transfer)`. If your
note says 24 plants, you have looked at `seedlings`, not `transfer`.
:::

## Solution recipes

The file `data/solutions.csv` lists six solutions that we will calculate with
later. Each row gives a solution ID, the dissolved substance (`solute`), its mass
in g, its molar mass in g/mol, and the final volume in mL. As on day 6, a
**mole** is a unit of amount of substance and the molar mass says how many grams
one mole weighs.

1. Read the file into `solutions`. Before running `str()`, predict which columns
   are text and which are numbers, then check. `solution_id` and `solute` are text;
   the other three are numbers.
2. Use `dim()`, `unique(solutions$solute)` and `sum(is.na())` to find out how many
   solutions there are, which substances, and whether anything is missing:
   **6 rows, 5 columns**, two substances (`sodium-chloride` and `glucose`), nothing
   missing.
3. Use `range()` on `mass_g` and `molar_mass_g_mol` to find out how far each
   varies: masses from **0.2922 to 2.7024 g**, molar masses **58.44 and 180.16
   g/mol**. Both columns are numbers, but they measure different things, so adding
   a mass to a molar mass would be meaningless.
4. Save `reports/solutions-import-audit.txt`: the size of the table, what each
   column means and its unit, and the rule you will use later: amount (mol) =
   mass / molar mass, concentration = amount / final volume in litres.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why is the header not a plant?

The header line holds the column names. `dim()` counts only the 24 data rows.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why can R not tell whether the lengths are in mm or cm?

The file contains only names and numbers. Units are written in the dictionary,
by people. That is why the column names end in `_mm`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why does `day07.R` also work in a classmate's project folder?

It uses the relative path `data/seedlings.csv`, which starts from whatever project
folder is open, not a path containing your user name.
:::

**Keep:** `day07.R`. Next: [calculate growth and draw a figure](08-transform-plot.qmd).
